A (Introduction to Fields)

Words: 392 Articles: 13
2009 OurBigBook.com

A2

Words: 392 Articles: 12
A OurBigBook.com
The characteristic is the least positive integer r with r1K​=0, if it exists, and zero otherwise. The prime subfield is the smallest subfield containing 1K​; in characteristic p it is F={0,1,…,(p−1)1K​}≅Fp​. Every field automorphism fixes 1K​ and addition, so it fixes every element of this prime subfield.

a

Words: 47 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 47
a OurBigBook.com
The additive sequence 0,1,2⋅1,… must repeat because K is finite, so the characteristic is positive. If its least positive value were composite, r=ab with 1<a,b<r, then (a1K​)(b1K​)=r1K​=0 while neither factor would be zero. A field has no zero divisors, giving a contradiction. Hence charK=p is prime​.

b

Words: 43 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 43
b OurBigBook.com
The finite field K is a finite-dimensional vector space over its prime subfield F of size p. A basis has some positive length n, and every element is uniquely specified by n coefficients in F. There are p choices per coefficient, so ∣K∣=pn​ and [K:F]=n.

i

Words: 43 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 43
i OurBigBook.com
Since K=F(λ) and the extension is finite, the element λ is algebraic. Its minimal polynomial is irreducible, and evaluation gives an isomorphism F[X]/(mλ​)≅F[λ]=F(λ)=K. If its degree is d, the powers 1,λ,…,λd−1 form a basis. Comparing with [K:F]=n gives degmλ​=n​.

ii

Words: 68 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 68
ii OurBigBook.com
Define ϑ(x)=xp on all of K. The binomial coefficients between the endpoints are divisible by p, so (x+y)p=xp+yp; also (xy)p=xpyp and 1p=1. Thus this is a field homomorphism. Its kernel is zero, and an injective self-map of the finite set K is surjective. Hence ϑ is an automorphism​, the Frobenius automorphism, with the required image of λ. It fixes F by the preceding prime-subfield argument.

iii

Words: 65 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 65
iii OurBigBook.com
Take 0<m<n, the intended positive-exponent range. If ϑm(λ)=λ, then ϑm fixes both F and its field generator, so it fixes every element of K=F(λ). Every element would then be a root of Xpm−X. But that polynomial has degree pm<pn=∣K∣, impossible for a nonzero polynomial over a field. Thus ϑm(λ)=λ(0<m<n)​. The source writes only m<n; zero must be excluded, since ϑ0(λ)=λ.

iv

Words: 79 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 79
iv OurBigBook.com
For nonzero x∈K, Lagrange's theorem in K× gives xpn−1=1; zero satisfies xpn=x too. Thus ϑn is the identity, and (iii) excludes every smaller positive order. Hence ∣⟨ϑ⟩∣=n​.
Any field automorphism of K fixes F and is determined by its value on λ. That value must be a root of the degree-n minimal polynomial, so there are at most n automorphisms. The n powers of ϑ already attain this bound. Consequently Aut(K)=⟨ϑ⟩≅Cn​​.

B (Group Theory)

Words: 465 Articles: 7
2009 OurBigBook.com

B2

Words: 465 Articles: 6
B OurBigBook.com

i

Words: 60 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 60
i OurBigBook.com
A left action is a map (g,ω)↦gω satisfying 1ω=ω and (gh)ω=g(hω). The orbit of ω is Gω={gω:g∈G}. The action is transitive when there is exactly one orbit on the nonempty acted-on set, equivalently when any point can be moved to any other by a group element. An action is equivalently a homomorphism from G to the permutation group of the set.

ii

Words: 239 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 239
ii OurBigBook.com
Act by left multiplication on the five cosets of H. The kernel is the core ⋂g∈G​gHg−1, a normal subgroup contained in H, so the hypothesis makes it trivial. Thus G embeds in S5​, and its image has order 60 and index two. An index-two subgroup is normal, so the quotient is of order two. Every three-cycle maps trivially to that quotient, since its order divides three. Three-cycles generate A5​, so the image contains A5​; their equal order gives G≅A5​​.
For completeness, prove simplicity rather than merely invoking it. The nonidentity even cycle types in S5​ are three-cycles, products of two disjoint transpositions and five-cycles. In A5​, a three-cycle has centralizer of order three, so its conjugacy class has size 20. A double transposition has centralizer of order four in A5​, giving class size 15. A five-cycle has centralizer its cyclic subgroup of order five, giving class size 12; the 24 such elements therefore split into two classes of size 12. These account for all 60 elements with the identity.
A normal subgroup is a union of whole conjugacy classes, containing the identity, and its order must divide 60. No nonempty proper sum of the class sizes 15,20,12,12, plus one, is a divisor of 60 greater than one: the possible proper nontrivial sums are 13,16,21,25,28,33,36,40,45,48. Only the full union has order 60. Hence A5​ is simple​, and so is G.

iii

Words: 166 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 166
iii OurBigBook.com
Choose one regular tetrahedron inscribed in the dodecahedron and let H be its stabilizer among rotations of the dodecahedron. The twelve rotations of that tetrahedron preserve the dodecahedron; geometrically these are its identity, eight rotations by ±2π/3 about tetrahedral vertex axes and three half-turns about opposite tetrahedral edge axes. They act faithfully on its four vertices and give the twelve even permutations. Thus H≅A4​,∣H∣=12​ without using part (ii).
To check the core condition geometrically, the fifteen half-turns of the dodecahedron, about opposite-edge-midpoint axes, are conjugate under its rotations. A normal subgroup contained in H cannot contain even one of these half-turns, because normality would then force all fifteen into a group of order twelve. On the other hand every nontrivial normal subgroup of A4​ contains a half-turn: if it contains a three-cycle, its conjugates and their inverses generate A4​; otherwise its nonidentity elements are among the three double transpositions, which are conjugate in A4​. Apply this observation to any normal subgroup of the full rotation group lying inside H. It must be trivial, proving exactly the required condition.

For an odd prime p, the Legendre symbol is (a/p)=0​ if p∣a, (a/p)=1​ if a is a nonzero square modulo p, and (a/p)=−1​ otherwise. It depends only on the residue class of a.

ii

Words: 34 Articles: 1
C2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 34
ii OurBigBook.com
Euler's criterion states that for p∤a,
a(p−1)/2≡(pa​)(modp).​
(1)
For a multiple of p, both the Legendre symbol and that positive power vanish modulo p, so the congruence extends to that case as well.

iii

Words: 22 Articles: 1
C2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 22
iii OurBigBook.com
Gauss's lemma for quadratic residues states: if p∤a and m is the number of least positive residue classes among a,2a,…,((p−1)/2)a that exceed p/2, then (a/p)=(−1)m​.

iv

Words: 40 Articles: 1
C2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 40
iv OurBigBook.com
For a=2 the displayed multiples are 2,4,…,p−1, already least positive residue classes. Those greater than p/2 correspond to j>p/4. Thus their number is m=(p−1)/2−⌊p/4⌋. For p≡1,3,5,7(mod8), its parity is respectively even, odd, odd, even. Gauss's lemma therefore gives
(p2​)={1,−1,​p≡1,7(mod8),p≡3,5(mod8).​​
(2)

v

Words: 17 Articles: 1
C2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 17
v OurBigBook.com
Euler's criterion gives (−1/p)=(−1)(p−1)/2. The Legendre symbol is multiplicative, so multiplying this sign by the result of (iv) yields
(p−2​)={1,−1,​p≡1,3(mod8),p≡5,7(mod8).​​
(3)

vi

Words: 120 Articles: 1
C2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 120
vi OurBigBook.com
Suppose there are only finitely many primes p1​,…,pr​≡3(mod8), and let N be their product. This is odd, so N2+2≡3(mod8). No listed prime divides this number, since reduction modulo any pi​ gives two. Every prime divisor q is odd and does not divide N, and satisfies N2≡−2(modq). Thus (−2/q)=1, forcing q≡1 or 3(mod8) by (v).
A product of prime factors all congruent to one modulo eight could not be three modulo eight. More precisely, the product of factors congruent to three is three modulo eight exactly when their total exponent is odd. Thus at least one prime divisor q≡3(mod8) occurs. It is not in the alleged complete list, a contradiction. Hence there are infinitely many primes congruent to three modulo eight.

i

Solution
Words: 73
i OurBigBook.com
For product measure spaces, Tonelli's theorem states that for a nonnegative measurable function the product-space integral equals either iterated integral, allowing the value +∞. Fubini's theorem states that if a measurable function has finite integral of its absolute value, then its sections are integrable almost everywhere, both iterated integrals exist and equal the product-space integral. The absolute-integrability hypothesis is what permits this conclusion for a signed function. These statements apply to the Lebesgue product spaces used here, which are sigma-finite.

ii OurBigBook.com
The function g is measurable, and for fixed positive y both terms are integrable over 0<x<1 by linear substitution and integrability of f. Those substitutions give
∫01​g(x,y)dx=y1​(∫0y​f(t)dt−∫0ay​f(t)dt)=−y1​∫yay​f(t)dt<0.
(6)
The strict sign follows from positivity of f on a nonempty interval, since a>1. Similarly each section in y is absolutely integrable for fixed x>0, and
∫1∞​g(x,y)dy=x1​(∫x∞​f(t)dt−∫ax∞​f(t)dt)=x1​∫xax​f(t)dt>0.
(7)
If g were absolutely integrable on the stated rectangle, Fubini would make the two finite iterated integrals equal. The first would be strictly negative and the second strictly positive, which is impossible. Therefore g∈/L1((0,1)×(1,∞))​. The one-dimensional section integrability does not rescue the missing product-space hypothesis.

The function h is measurable and nonnegative. In first-quadrant polar coordinates, including the Jacobian, its integral is
(∫0∞​e−r2r3dr)(∫0π/2​(cosθ)3/2(sinθ)1/2dθ).
(8)
The radial factor is 1/2 by the supplied fact and the angular integrand is at most one, giving finiteness. The nonnegative change-of-variables formula is valid before finiteness is known, and this bound proves h∈L1.
Fubini may now factor the Cartesian integral. Substituting u=x2, v=y2 in the respective factors gives
∬hdxdy=41​(∫0∞​e−uu1/4du)(∫0∞​e−vv−1/4dv).
(9)
Both are finite: their powers at zero exceed −1, and the exponential controls infinity. Comparing with the polar expression proves
∫0π/2​(cosθ)3/2(sinθ)1/2dθ=21​Γ(5/4)Γ(3/4),​
(10)
which is exactly the product of integrals requested.

A subset U of a metric space is open if for every x∈U there exists r>0 with Bd​(x,r)⊆U, where Bd​(x,r)={y:d(x,y)<r}. The radius may depend on the point. The empty set is open vacuously.

Words: 35 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 35
ii OurBigBook.com
Continuity at x means that for every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that dX​(x,y)<δ implies dY​(f(x),f(y))<ε for every y∈X. Equivalently, the inverse image of each neighborhood of f(x) is a neighborhood of x.

Solution

The map is continuous if it is continuous at every point of its domain. Equivalently the inverse image of every open subset of Y is open in X. These equivalent formulations use the given metrics' induced topologies.

da​(x,z)=rx​+rz​≤(rx​+ry​)+(ry​+rz​)=da​(x,y)+da​(y,z).

It is path-connected: two points can be joined by a polygonal path avoiding the missing point. Thus all equivalence classes are connected.
The projection π is continuous and onto, since (z,z+1)∈X. If U is open in X, it is open in C2 because X is open. Product-coordinate projection is open: around any (z,w)∈U there is a product of open disks contained in U, whose first disk is a neighborhood inside π(U). Hence π(U) is open.
Its fibers are precisely the equivalence classes, so it induces a bijection πˉ:X/R→C. Continuity follows from the quotient topology and π=πˉ∘q. If V is open in X/R, then q−1(V) is open in X and πˉ(V)=π(q−1(V)) is open. Thus the inverse is continuous too, proving X/R≅C​ as topological spaces. The plane is connected, so the connected-fiber equivalence in (b)(ii) gives X is connected​.

The phrase “of degree n” denotes membership in Πn​ here: the actual degree may be smaller, for example for constant data.

If the result is zero, part (a)'s uniqueness for the zero interpolation data forces every coefficient to be zero. Thus the square matrix has trivial kernel and is invertible. Equivalently the interpolation map is a linear bijection between two spaces of dimension n+1.

Repeated application of Rolle's theorem gives an interior point ξ where H(n+1)(ξ)=0. As pn(n+1)​=0 and ω(n+1)=(n+1)!, this gives C=f(n+1)(ξ)/(n+1)!. Therefore

Every derivative of order n+1 of sin2x has magnitude at most 2n+1. Pair the symmetric nodes a=i/n and 1−a. For 0≤x,a≤1,
∣(x−a)(x−(1−a))∣=∣(x−1/2)2−(a−1/2)2∣≤1/4.

∥f−pn​∥∞​≤(n+1)!2⌊(n+1)/2⌋​.​

The bound tends to zero by factorial growth, so pn​→f uniformly on [0,1]​. This conclusion uses smoothness of this particular function and does not assert uniform convergence of equispaced interpolation for arbitrary continuous data.

Solution
Words: 166
d OurBigBook.com
Proceed column by column. At stage j=1,…,n−2, consider the entries below the diagonal in column j, indexed j+1,…,n. If this tail is nonzero, part (c) provides a Householder matrix sending it to a multiple of its first coordinate vector. Embed this matrix as an orthogonal matrix acting identically on coordinates 1,…,j, and apply the similarity transformation A↦QjT​AQj​. The tail's entries below row j+1 become zero. Symmetry is preserved, so the corresponding entries in row j vanish too. If the tail is already zero, use the identity transformation.
Earlier reduced columns remain unchanged in their required zero positions: all their entries in the newly mixed tail coordinates were already zero, and the first j coordinates are fixed. Thus each stage preserves the previous zeros while creating the next ones. After n−2 stages, all entries at distance greater than one from the diagonal vanish. With the product Q=Q1​⋯Qn−2​ one has QTQ=I and
QTAQ is symmetric tridiagonal.​
(52)
This constructive reduction uses only reflections on successive trailing subspaces.

i

Words: 200 Articles: 1
R2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 200
i OurBigBook.com
Use the equivalent bipartite formulation: the left set has m vertices and a matching must cover it. Necessity is immediate, since distinct matched partners for any left subset must all lie in its neighborhood.
For sufficiency, induct on m. The cases zero and one are immediate from the neighborhood condition. If a nonempty proper left subset A satisfies ∣N(A)∣=∣A∣, induction matches A into N(A). For the remaining left vertices and remaining right vertices, any subset B has at least ∣B∣ available neighbors: applying Hall's inequality to A∪B and removing the ∣A∣ possible neighbors in N(A) proves this. Induction supplies the second matching, and the two combine.
If no nonempty proper subset has equality, all such subsets have at least one extra neighbor. Choose any left vertex and one of its neighbors and match them. After deleting the pair, each nonempty subset of the remaining left side originally was proper and had at least ∣B∣+1 neighbors; losing the chosen right vertex leaves at least ∣B∣. Induction completes the matching. Thus
∣N(A)∣≥∣A∣ for every left subset A​
(53)
is sufficient as well as necessary. If the right set is infinite, any subset with infinitely many neighbors automatically meets the finite inequalities, and the same finite-left induction applies.

ii OurBigBook.com
A complete matching from V1​ to V2​ is a set of edges with no shared endpoints that contains an edge incident to every vertex of V1​. The theorem in (i) gives the necessary and sufficient condition
∣N(A)∣≥∣A∣for every A⊆V1​.​
(54)
The intended setting is a finite left vertex set; no condition that every vertex of V2​ be used is imposed.

Form a bipartite graph with left labels 1,…,m, right set E, and an edge i−e exactly when e∈Si​. A matching covering all left labels is precisely a choice of distinct representatives. Its neighborhood condition is
​i∈I⋃​Si​​≥∣I∣for every I⊆{1,…,m}.​
(55)
Thus this is necessary and sufficient. The underlying set E may be infinite; only the number of sets to be represented is finite.

The missing sets in the five columns are {4,5}, {1,3}, {4,5}, {2,3} and {1,2}. One choice of distinct representatives is (4,1,5,3,2), giving the fourth row. Each column then has exactly one missing number, producing the fifth row (5,3,4,2,1). A completed square is
​12345​24513​31254​45132​53421​​.​
(56)
Every row and column contains each number from one to five once. The construction explicitly chooses from the missing sets, so it preserves all entries of the given rectangle.

v

Words: 121 Articles: 1
R2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 121
v OurBigBook.com
For an m×n rectangle, let Sj​ be the symbols absent from column j. Each has size n−m. Across all columns, each symbol is absent exactly n−m times, because it appears once in each existing row. For any set J of columns, count incidences between those columns and their missing symbols. There are ∣J∣(n−m) incidences, while each distinct symbol in the union contributes at most n−m. Therefore ∣⋃j∈J​Sj​∣≥∣J∣.
Hall's theorem supplies distinct representatives, one per column, forming an additional row with all n symbols. This extends the rectangle without any column repetition. Repeat with m+1 rows, then successively until there are n rows. Hence every finite latin rectangle extends to a Latin square by adding the required rows.

a OurBigBook.com
Let Zp​=∑x​p~​(x) and Zq​=∑x​q~​(x), both finite and positive as required for normalization. A sufficient envelope condition is M≥x∈Ωsup​p~​(x)/q~​(x)​ with finite M>0. Use independent proposals and independent uniforms on each trial. This guarantees an acceptance probability in [0,1] for every state. Choose the smallest certified upper bound on that ratio, since increasing M decreases the overall acceptance rate. The ratio must be bounded for this particular proposal to admit such an envelope.

b

Words: 60 Articles: 1
S2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 60
b OurBigBook.com
For one proposal, P(Y=x,accept)=q(x)p~​(x)/(Mq~​(x))=p~​(x)/(MZq​). Summing gives total acceptance probability a=Zp​/(MZq​)>0. Conditioning on acceptance therefore gives P(Y=x∣accept)=p~​(x)/Zp​=p(x).
The first accepted result has this law too: the probability of k−1 failures followed by acceptance at x is (1−a)k−1p~​(x)/(MZq​). Sum the geometric series over k≥1 to obtain P(X=x)=p(x)​. Positive acceptance probability also proves almost-sure termination.

c

Words: 46 Articles: 1
S2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 46
c OurBigBook.com
Each Ni​ is geometric on {1,2,…} with success probability a=Zp​/(MZq​). Hence
E[Ni​]=Zp​MZq​​,Zq​/Zp​​=MN1​i=1∑N​ni​.​
(57)
Linearity of expectation proves the estimator is unbiased. Moreover the joint probability factors:
P(Ni​=k,Xi​=x)=(1−a)k−1MZq​p~​(x)​=[(1−a)k−1a]p(x).
(58)
Thus Ni​ and Xi​ are independent​, not merely uncorrelated. Fresh independent trials make the simulated cycles independent as well.

d

Words: 99 Articles: 1
S2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 99
d OurBigBook.com
A fixed proposal-count budget does not bias the accepted values. For each trial, acceptance has probability a, and conditional on acceptance its label has law p independently of the other trials. Conditional on the full accept/reject pattern among the first N∗ proposals, the successful labels are independent with common law p. Therefore K∼Binomial(N∗,a), and conditional on K=k, the k retained samples are independent draws from p. When K=0 there is simply no sample. This concerns a budget fixed independently of the proposal values; it does not assert that an empirical average is defined on an empty output.

e

Words: 134 Articles: 1
S2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 134
e OurBigBook.com
State-dependent execution times can bias the finite set of completed outputs. A simple counterexample takes p=q uniform on two states and M=1, so every proposal is accepted. Suppose processing the first state takes one unit of time and processing the second takes two. Stop at a deadline between one and two units, discarding any unfinished computation. The only possible completed output is the first state; conditional on obtaining a sample, its law is concentrated there rather than uniform.
This demonstrates that a wall-clock cutoff can select outputs according to their processing cost, unlike the fixed proposal budget in (d). It does not imply a permanent asymptotic bias of averages over an indefinitely growing completed sequence: the finite-horizon stopping and censoring are the issue. Without assumptions relating runtime to states, exact finite-sample unbiasedness cannot be guaranteed.
